chunks.text: TL;DR
Google reads six schema.org types first for restaurant pages, Restaurant, Menu, OpeningHoursSpecification, AggregateRating, Reservation, F A Q.
Most independent restaurant sites have two of the six. The other four are missing or malformed.
Each missing type is a different Google surface you are not eligible for: local-pack card, AI Overview citation, Reserve button, rich snippet, holiday-hours badge.
Schema rots quietly when C M S or template updates touch the templates. A monthly schema check catches the drift before the reviews do.

Here is a rich result that never showed. A 60-seat Italian place ships a homepage with a stars block, an hours block, a menu block, all present, all in the (code) , all stamped by the theme. The owner pastes the U R L into the validator and one line comes back red: "priceRnge": "$" . A four-letter typo. Google reads the whole block as malformed and renders a plain blue link, no stars, no price chip, no Reserve button, for the eight months nobody thinks to re-check. The schema was there the entire time. It just didn’t work , and “present” and “working” are the two words this whole guide lives between.

That is the failure this teardown is built to catch. The honest version of restaurant schema markup is six schema.org types, Restaurant, Menu, OpeningHoursSpecification, AggregateRating, Reservation, and F A Q, and the job is less “add schema” than “tear down the broken block your C M S already stamped and paste the one Google can actually read.” Most independent sites have two of the six working; the other four are missing, or present-but-malformed in exactly the way the typo above is, valid-looking, silently disqualified.

Each broken or absent type is a different surface in Google’s results you’re not eligible for, the local-pack card, AI Overview citations, the Reserve button, the rich snippet, the holiday-hours badge. So the gap between “some schema markup ” and “all six, working” isn’t linear. Below: the broken block torn down beside the fixed one for each of the six types, what Google reads from each, and the validator pass that tells you which version you’re actually running.

How Google reads a restaurant page, in two passes, and why schema is the second pass. Pass one: the crawler reads your visible prose, the menu text, the hours line, the About paragraph. It guesses you are a restaurant, but it has to infer your cuisine, your price band, and your hours from sentences written for humans, and it guesses wrong often. Pass two: the crawler reads your Json-LD, the invisible structured block. Now the same facts arrive labeled, type Restaurant, servesCuisine Italian, priceRange one dollar sign, opens seventeen hundred. No inference, no guessing. The third beat is what changes on the results page: the labeled facts are what Google is willing to render as stars, an open-now chip, a price chip, and a Reserve button, because it now trusts them enough to show them. The prose alone gets you a plain blue link; the schema is what unlocks the rich result. That is the whole mechanism this guide installs.
1. Restaurant, the foundational type.

This is the one you cannot skip. Restaurant schema tells Google what business type you are, your address, your phone, your price range , and a handful of other facts that determine whether you appear in queries like "Italian restaurants near me" at all.
Minimum viable Json-LD:

The minimum viable Restaurant block: type Restaurant, name, image U R L, phone, price range, a PostalAddress object with street, locality, region, postal code, country, a servesCuisine array, and acceptsReservations as True or False. Without this block, every other schema you ship sits orphaned, Google has nothing to attach the menu, hours, or reviews to.

The servesCuisine array is doing more work than people realize, it is how Google knows to show you for cuisine-specific queries. Do not put more than two cuisines unless you actually serve them; ambiguity demotes you in queries you should win.
2. Menu, the type most restaurants fake.

This is the most common teardown of the six. Almost every restaurant site has either no Menu schema at all, or the platform stamped the entire menu as one text string, the whole carte jammed into a single field. It validates. It is also useless: Google can’t parse individual dishes out of a blob, so you don’t rank for "tacos al pastor near me" at the dish level, and the AI Overviews have nothing to lift.
Here is the broken block your builder probably stamped, torn down beside the structured one that actually ranks. Read what Google gets from each:

A teardown of Menu schema, broken next to fixed. The broken version, what most platforms stamp: an @type Menu whose entire menu is a single text field, a comma-run of dish names and prices, tacos al pastor fourteen dollars, carnitas thirteen, all jammed into one string. It validates, but Google reads it as one undifferentiated text blob, so no dish ranks on its own and the AI Overviews have nothing to quote. The fixed version: the same dishes nested as hasMenuSection wrapping hasMenuItem entries, each item carrying a name, a description, and an Offer with price and currency. Now Google reads tacos al pastor as a distinct dish with a distinct description and price. The description field is the one doing the most work, it is what Google's AI Overviews lift verbatim when someone asks what the tacos al pastor are like at your restaurant. The difference between the two blocks is not validity, both pass. The difference is whether Google can see one dish or only a wall of text.

The description matters more than the name, that is the field Google's AI Overviews lift verbatim when someone asks "what are tacos al pastor like at Bistro Petit." An empty description, or a dish swallowed into the blob above, earns no AI citation.

The same restaurant query in Google, with and without the six schema types shipped. Without schema: a bare blue link, just the page title, the U R L, and a meta description. No stars, no price range, no open-now indicator, no map pin, no Reserve button. With schema: the same title and U R L, plus a four point seven star rating with four hundred twelve reviews, a dollar-sign price chip, an open-now indicator showing closes at ten PM, a map-pack pin, and a Reserve a Table button. Same page, same meta description, the schema is what surfaces the six new elements.
3. OpeningHoursSpecification, the one that costs you walk-ins.

If your hours are wrong on Google, your hours are wrong everywhere. OpeningHoursSpecification is the schema that powers the "Open now" / "Closes at 10 PM" badge on your search panel, and the one that gets stale when you change Sunday hours and forget to update the site.

An openingHoursSpecification array, one entry per day-of-week group. dayOfWeek is an array of weekday names; opens and closes are twenty-four-hour strings. The cost of skipping this is direct, customers see 'hours unavailable' on the Google panel and walk past. Holiday overrides go in a separate specialOpeningHoursSpecification block, which is the most common reason an angry-on-Christmas-Eve review lands.

Holiday overrides go in a separate specialOpeningHoursSpecification block, both Google and Apple Maps read it, and a missing holiday closure is the most common reason an angry-on-Christmas-Eve review lands. The failure mode worth naming: C M S or template updates can quietly strip Json-LD overnight. If you do not have a monthly schema check on your calendar, the first time you will know your hours block went missing is when the one-star reviews start arriving.
Run Schema Checker on your homepage to see whether your current hours schema is valid; Open Hours generates the Json-LD if you need a fresh start.

Four field-level mistakes disqualify a block the way the hours example does, quietly, with no error a human notices. Each has a torn-down twin: the field as builders leave it, and the field as Google needs it.
From the floor

The one I check first on any block, before I read a single property, is the hours. Not because it’s the most important type, it’s because it’s the type that rots without anyone touching the code. I changed our Sunday close by an hour for a private event one December, updated the G B P, and forgot the Json-LD sat in a separate template. For two weeks the site said one thing and the panel said another, and the only reason I caught it was a guest who showed up to a locked door and left the one-star that told me. Now the hours block is the first line of a monthly fifteen-minute walk I do on the first of the month. The teardown you do once; the drift is forever, so the calendar reminder is the actual fix.
4. AggregateRating, the one that boosts Ctr by double digits.
If you have reviews on your own site, AggregateRating shows up as the gold-star pattern in your search snippet. The Ctr lift is real, typically 8-15% for restaurant queries.

An AggregateRating block with ratingValue and reviewCount, a four point seven rating across four hundred twelve reviews. This is what puts the gold stars in your search snippet, and the click-through lift is typically eight to fifteen percent on restaurant queries. The constraint: the reviews have to be on your own site. Aggregating Google's reviews into your own AggregateRating violates Google's policy and earns a manual action.

The constraint: the reviews have to be on your site . You cannot aggregate Google's reviews into your own AggregateRating, that violates Google's structured-data policies and can earn a manual action that takes weeks to lift.
5. Reservation, the one that unlocks Find a Table.

If you are on OpenTable, Resy, Tock, or SevenRooms, your reservation system already publishes the right schema. But if your booking is a custom form on your own site, you need to publish Reservation schema yourself, otherwise Google cannot show the "Reserve a table" button in your panel.
The integration with Find a Table requires this schema to be valid And your booking endpoint to be publicly reachable. Check both with Schema Checker .
F A Q schema is the cheapest AI-citation surface a restaurant has. The fact that almost nobody ships it is the opportunity.
6. F A Q, the AI-citation magnet.

F A Q schema is not restaurant-specific, but it is the highest-leverage AI-citation surface for restaurant pages. ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google's AI Overviews read F A Q blocks first when answering operational questions.

An FAQPage block with mainEntity holding Question and Answer pairs. Each Question has a name field, the literal question, and an acceptedAnswer with a text field holding your reply. This is the format AI assistants pull verbatim into citations. Write the answer the way you'd want to see it quoted back to a customer.
Six well-written F A Q entries, actually useful operational questions, not marketing copy, typically lift AI-search-driven traffic 20-40% within 60 days.

Schema coverage on a typical restaurant site, by type. Restaurant: about eighty percent of sites have it, usually present but often incomplete. Menu: about twenty-five percent parse, most are string blobs or missing entirely. OpeningHoursSpecification: about sixty percent are valid; the rest are stale. AggregateRating: about thirty percent present; the rest absent. Reservation: about forty percent present, almost always auto-published by OpenTable, Resy, or Tock. F A Q: about fifteen percent present, rarest of the six. The pattern: the most operator-friendly schema, F A Q, is also the one almost nobody ships, which is why it’s the highest-leverage edit in twenty twenty-six.
How to check what you have today.

To check your restaurant schema, view-source the live page and search for application/ld+json to confirm a block exists, then paste the page U R L into validator.schema.org to confirm it passes with no red errors. “Present” is not the same as “working”, the more common failure is schema that is technically on the page but silently disqualified, so walk the four questions below in order; the first “no” is your problem.

A four-question diagnostic for finding the schema type that is silently broken even though it is on the page. Question one: is there a Json-LD script tag in the rendered head at all? If no, nothing downstream matters, the C M S or a template update stripped it, and that is the whole problem. Question two: does the validator pass with no red errors? A single unknown property or a missing required field disqualifies the whole block, so the stars never appear even though the rating value is right there. Question three: is the AggregateRating sourced from reviews on your own site rather than aggregated from Google? Aggregating Google's reviews violates policy and earns a manual action that pulls the stars and takes weeks to lift. Question four: does your name, address, and phone match across the site, Google Business Profile, and Yelp? If the N A P conflicts, valid schema still loses the local pack to the more coherent competitor, because schema cannot paper over a contradiction. The first no is the fix.

Run your homepage through Schema Checker . It returns a present/valid/missing verdict for each of these six types and points at the broken pieces. Save the result to your Restaurant Audit and re-run monthly, schema rots when C M S updates touch templates.

The compounding argument: each missing schema type is a different Google surface you are not eligible for. The six types together unlock the local-pack card, AI Overview citations, the Reserve button, the rich snippet, and the holiday-hours badge. Add them in order, and the cumulative effect on impressions usually lands somewhere between 20% and 60% within a quarter.

The move is: ship Restaurant + OpeningHours + Menu this week, F A Q next, and let AggregateRating + Reservation come from your booking platform. Six types in roughly two weeks of deliberate work. The surfaces queue up behind them.
Schema is not optional. Each missing type is a Google surface you have voluntarily disqualified yourself from.
The complete, paste-ready Restaurant Json-LD.

The six types above describe what Google can use. This section is the how, a single production-grade Json-LD payload that ships Restaurant + Menu + OpeningHoursSpecification + F A Q together, in the validated shape that drops into the (code) of a restaurant page. Adapt the values to your own restaurant, validate, deploy.
How to use it.
Three steps:
Copy the block below into a single (code) tag inside your <head>. One tag, not six.
Change the seven fields marked // Edit : the restaurant name, address parts (street, city, region, zip), phone, opening hours, and the menu items.
Validate at validator.schema.org by pasting the U R L of your page. Fix anything red. Most errors are missing commas or stray quotes.
The complete example.

Below is a complete worked schema for an illustrative 60-seat Dmv Italian restaurant. The structure nests six types: Restaurant (root), Menu, OpeningHoursSpecification, AggregateRating, Reservation, and F A Q. Each one unlocks a different Google surface (per the six-types article). Save it as a starting point; tighten as needed.
That’s 60 lines of Json-LD covering the six types Google reads first on a restaurant page. The seven // Edit fields are everything you have to change to make it yours.

The same restaurant's Google result, before and after the paste-ready schema. Before: a bare blue-link result, title 'Roma Cucina, Italian Restaurant in Silver Spring,' the U R L, and a meta description. No stars, no hours, no map pin. After: the same title and U R L, plus a four point six star rating with four hundred twelve reviews, a price-range chip showing two dollar signs, an open-now indicator with closes at ten p m, a map-pack pin with directions, and a Reserve a table button. Six new surface elements added to one search result by sixty lines of Json-LD.
Before you publish.
Three checks. Each one catches a class of error that’s otherwise invisible until you’re wondering why the local-pack still hasn’t shown you.

Run it through validator.schema.org . Paste your page U R L. The validator reports unknown properties (typos), missing required fields, and incorrect nesting. Fix the red items. Yellow is usually fine to ship.

Confirm the rendered page matches . Open your page in a browser, view-source, search for application/ld+json . Confirm the script tag is there and the Json is what you expect. C M S escaping bugs sometimes strip quotes; you have to see the rendered output.

Test with Google’s Rich Results test . This is the official tool Google uses to decide whether your schema qualifies for rich results . It tells you which surfaces your schema is eligible for. Run it after the validator passes.

The four-step paste, test, wait, verify workflow after pasting the schema. Step one: paste the Json-LD into the head of every public page, not just the homepage. Step two: run Google's Rich Results Test on three URLs and fix every red error before walking away. Step three: wait seven to fourteen days for the re-crawl, Googlebot needs to see the schema in production before any feature appears. Step four: verify in Search Console under Enhancements, where each schema type gets its own report showing valid pages and errors.
What happens after you ship.

Don’t expect immediate effect. Google’s crawler may take 24, 72 hours to revisit your page and pick up the new schema. Some surfaces (the local-pack, AggregateRating stars) update within a week. Others (Reservation deep links via Find a Table, F A Q rich snippets) can take 30+ days. The longest-tail ones are the AI Overview citations, which can take 90 days to start landing.

Once it’s shipped, leave the schema alone. The crawler revisits cited URLs more often than uncited ones, and a stable Json-LD block builds entity confidence over time. Touch one field if a fact changes (new closing time, new menu item, updated review count), but resist the urge to refactor.

Rich-result appearance odds, ninety days after pasting the schema, by type. AggregateRating: gold stars in the snippet appear on roughly ninety percent of queries within thirty days. OpeningHoursSpecification: the open-now badge appears on roughly eighty-five percent of queries within thirty days. Restaurant plus PostalAddress: the local-pack card appears on roughly seventy percent of branded queries within sixty days. Menu: dish-level ranking and AI Overview citations appear on roughly fifty-five percent of dish-name queries within sixty days. FAQPage: the F A Q rich snippet appears on roughly forty percent of question-shaped queries within sixty days. ReserveAction: the Reserve a table button appears on roughly thirty-five percent of branded queries within ninety days.
Key takeaways
Restaurant schema is foundational, without it you may not appear for cuisine queries at all.
Menu schema with structured MenuItem + description fields is what AI Overviews quote verbatim.
OpeningHoursSpecification + specialOpeningHoursSpecification together prevent the "closed even though Google said open" review.
AggregateRating with reviews from your own site lifts Ctr by 8, 15% on restaurant queries; aggregating Google's reviews violates policy.
F A Q schema is the highest-leverage AI-citation surface on a restaurant page.
See which of the six types your site is missing.

Schema Checker runs your homepage through all six types and returns a present / valid / missing verdict for each. Save the result to your Workshop and re-run monthly, schema rots when C M S updates touch templates.
